#7683. Is Heat Escaping Your House? A RISION Thermal Imaging Camera Can Help

Drafty windows, cold walls and rising heating bills? The RISION Magic Series helps you spot potential trouble areas before they become expensive problems.

Sponsored By: RISIONThis piece was created in partnership with RISION, your go-to for thermal imaging cameras and smart sensing devices.

Imagine cranking up the thermostat on a freezing winter morning to get cozy, only to find that somehow your living room still feels chilly. Maybe there’s a draft coming from the windows, or one area never seems to warm up. Whatever the reason, you might be heating a home that’s letting the warmth escape—and paying through the nose for it.

According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s ENERGY STAR program, you can save an average of 15% on heating and cooling costs by sealing air leaks and adding insulation where it’s needed. The tricky part? Figuring out exactly where the problems are.

That’s where a thermal imaging camera comes in handy. Instead of guessing which windows need resealing or where insulation might be missing, you can use one to spot temperature differences and take a closer look.

I recently got my hands on both the RISION Magic and Magic Pro thermal cameras and spent time with them around my house. From scanning windows and exterior walls to checking HVAC vents and even tracking my own footprints across the carpet, I was impressed by how much these tiny cameras could reveal.

Better yet, both models are on sale for up to 45% off during Black Friday sales, making now an excellent time to pick one up.

A thermal imaging camera detects infrared radiation emitted by objects and turns this into a visual representation of surface temperatures. Warmer (red, orange) and cooler (blue, purple) areas appear in contrasting colors, allowing you to see temperature differences that you can’t see with your own eyes.

This opens up some useful possibilities for homeowners. Imagine scanning around a window and spotting a cooler section along the frame. That doesn’t automatically mean there’s an air leak, but it’s a good reason to check the weatherstripping, caulking or surrounding insulation.

You can also use thermal imaging to check on other common household issues:

But remember: thermal imaging isn’t a crystal ball. There can be several reasons for surface temperature differences, and the camera won’t tell you exactly what’s wrong behind a wall. Still, it can help narrow down the places worth checking out before you start ripping off trim or making repairs.

That’s the appeal of the RISION Magic Series. The camera plugs directly into a compatible USB-C smartphone, tablet or computer, so there’s no need to carry around a bulky device. This thing is about the size of a packet of mints.

I spent a couple of days with the RISION Magic and Magic Pro, and one of my favorite things about these cameras is how little effort it takes to get started.

There’s no tiresome setup process or annoying account registration. I took the camera out of its box, plugged it into my phone, downloaded the app and started viewing the thermal feed. The whole process took less than two minutes. Considering how many devices require an email address, password and account verification before you can use them, this was a refreshing change.

The app itself is just as straightforward. You get a live thermal image and simple buttons to capture a photo or record a video. That’s about all there is to it, and that’s all you really need.

I was super impressed by the camera’s sensitivity. As I walked around my house, I could actually see the residual warmth of my footprints on the carpet. Plugged-in electronics appeared as warm spots, while my air-conditioning vents stood out in deep blue against the warmer ceiling.

The app also automatically highlighted particularly hot and cold areas with temperature readouts, making it easy to identify points of interest without constantly examining the entire image. Every now and then, the hotter readouts were difficult to read because the red writing was so close to the red heat source, but a little shift in camera angle normally fixes it.

Editor’s note: Both cameras require a compatible USB-C device and RISION’s accompanying software. They do not support Lightning connectors.

The RISION Magic is a great entry point if you’re looking to investigate insulation problems, cold spots or other temperature-related issues around the house. It’s small enough to slip into a pocket and plugs directly into your phone’s USB-C port, so there’s no separate battery or bulky equipment to worry about.

It features a native 160-by-120-pixel thermal sensor, enhanced to 320-by-240 pixels using RISION’s QuadIR processing technology. There’s also a 25Hz refresh rate, which keeps the image reasonably smooth as you move the camera around.

During testing, I liked how clearly the thermal images showed the framing behind my exterior walls. I could easily make out the positions of wall studs thanks to the subtle temperature differences across the surface. As someone who’s occasionally had trouble getting consistent readings from traditional stud finders, I found this useful, though I’d still confirm stud locations before drilling.

I also scanned around my windows, looking for cold spots that might indicate gaps in the seals or in the surrounding insulation. Thankfully, I didn’t find any major areas of concern. My house is only about two years old, so that was reassuring.

The Magic makes this type of inspection quick and easy, even if you have no previous experience with thermal cameras.

If you’re regularly tackling home renovations, HVAC repairs or more technical troubleshooting, the RISION Magic Pro gives you an extra level of detail.

The main difference is image resolution. The Magic Pro features a native 256-by-192-pixel thermal sensor, enhanced to 512-by-384 pixels through QuadIR processing. This step-up in detail can make it easier to distinguish smaller temperature variations when examining electrical components, HVAC equipment or other mechanical systems.

It’s almost identical to the standard Magic; the only way you can tell them apart is the coloring on the units themself. They both work exactly the same way; the Pro version just offers higher resolution.

For a regular homeowner, the extra resolution could be useful during larger renovation projects or more thorough home inspections. But the real appeal is for contractors, HVAC technicians, appliance repair professionals and experienced DIYers who want more information from their thermal images.

One unexpectedly useful application I found while testing was identifying cooler patches on carpeting. Damp areas can appear noticeably colder than the surrounding floor, which could make the camera handy for investigating spills or even the occasional pet accident. It’s not a substitute for a moisture meter, but it can help you figure out where to look before a spill dries.

Winter is a good time to be checking your home’s insulation and draft problems, particularly when the temperature difference between indoors and outdoors makes cold spots easier to identify. And with Black Friday discounts on both RISION Magic Series cameras, you can pick up a useful tool at a discount.

A thermal camera won’t fix a drafty window or replace missing insulation, but it can help you figure out where to focus your efforts. And when you’re trying to keep your home comfortable without sending your heating bill through the roof, knowing where to start is half the battle.

#7682. The Best Shovels of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

The Best Black Friday Deals for the Home ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

By Mark Wolfe, Additional research provided by Michelle Ullman, Timothy Dale

The smell of freshly turned earth, the weight of a sturdy shovel, and the view of bedding plants waiting to be placed into the ground can be sources of joy for many gardeners. But knowing which type of shovel is best for the landscaping project on your list may not be as easy as it seems. To help you make a good choice, we tested 10 highly rated shovels and consulted an expert for insights into selecting the right one.

Based on our efforts, we chose the Bully Tools 12-Gauge Round Point Shovel as the best overall option. It’s comfortable in hand, easy to use, and offers excellent performance in a variety of tasks. Still, other garden tools could be better for certain projects, and the rest of the shovels on our list are all great options. Read on to learn how each performed in our tests before choosing one of the best shovels for your gardening needs.

Bottom line: Choosing the right shovel depends on your specific gardening needs, with top picks offering versatility, value, and specialized functionality.

The following reviews of our tested top picks can help you decide which shovel is right for digging tasks like planting a vegetable garden or caring for your landscape. the materials that make it more durable in tough applications. While the extra weight might be worth it in some situations, a few extra pounds can make a noticeable difference after several hours of yard work. Ultimately, the ideal weight depends on the user’s own strength and endurance.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Comfort 4/5; Performance 4.3/5; Value 4.7/5

Long-handle round-point (LHRP) shovels are the most widely used shovels for general-purpose digging. When this Bully Tools LHRP performed consistently well across all our testing tasks, we knew it was the right choice for our award for best overall.

This model’s stout 12-gauge head powered through hard-packed clay soil and cut cleanly through sod and roots. We appreciated how easy the wide step area made it to use, even though we were wearing soft-soled shoes instead of work boots. And since the handle has a cushioned grip and enough flexibility to absorb the shock of digging without bending under a load of soil, we felt both comfortable and in control as we worked.

One possible downside of this option is that, while it has welded reinforcements for added strength, the area where the socket meets the blade doesn’t seem all that durable. If you try too hard to pry out a rock or thick root (which you should not do), it seems possible that the metal surrounding the weld could break.

This is our go-to shovel since it’s highly efficient for most yard and garden tasks. While it’s not the cheapest option, its versatility and overall excellent performance make it well worth the price.

Get the Bully Tools shovel at Amazon, Tractor Supply Co., The Home Depot, Northern Tool + Equipment, or Bully Tools.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Comfort 4/5; Performance 4/5; Value 4.7/5

This long-handle round-point shovel from Ames punches above its weight. It features a durable steel-reinforced fiberglass handle with a padded nonslip grip for outstanding comfort and control. The steel blade has an oversized step area and an open socket that’s reinforced with a steel collet. And all this comes at a value price.

Though it costs about half as much as our top pick, this Ames shovel weighs just over a pound less, making it a better all-purpose option for projects that don’t require heavy-duty reinforcements. The thinner steel used in the shovel head adds to its lightness but also allows it to flex slightly, so it is less aggressive in hard-packed clay soil and subject to more wear and tear in rocky ground. It’s also reinforced with an inner layer of steel to help resist cracking at the stress points, but the open-back handle sock seems like a possible failure point.

Get the Ames round-point shovel at The Home Depot or Walmart.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Comfort 5/5; Performance 4/5; Value 4.3/5

The Corona trench shovel is purpose-built for digging narrow trenches in any type of soil, making it essential for installing irrigation lines, running power for landscape lighting, and creating planting furrows for gardening. Since its 12-gauge steel blade is only 4 inches wide, it removes less than half the width of a round-point digging shovel. This unique design is ideal for precision digging, ensuring you don’t waste time and energy removing more dirt than is necessary.

In our tests, this trench shovel performed exceptionally well in heavy clay soil, maneuvering smoothly around rocks.  It also has a high-angle closed-handle socket that makes it easy to scoop out a flat trench bottom, while the lightweight hardwood handle provides excellent strength and shock resistance. Unlike some “cleanout”-style trench shovels, this one does not have raised sides to hold in a large volume of loose material, but it digs a new trench in packed earth more efficiently than a cleanout shovel could.

Get the Corona Tools shovel at Tractor Supply Co., Ace Hardware, or Corona Tools.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 3.75/5; Comfort 5/5; Performance 4.6/5; Value 4.3/5

When you’re planting a tree or transplanting a shrub, you need a shovel that can contend with packed soil, random rocks, and tough roots. The Spear Head Spade gardening shovel is designed with those tough tasks in mind. Its unique spearhead-shaped blade is made of hardened manganese steel and features a wide step and sharp edge, allowing it to find its way naturally to the path of least resistance and slice cleanly through roots. The open-back socket is reinforced with a steel collet and rubber gasket to boost strength and reduce shock. The straight fiberglass handle has two padded nonslip grips for superior comfort and control.

We tested the Spear Head Spade alongside similar digging tools like shovels and spades. It worked as well as any of those other hand garden tools, loosening and scooping like a digging shovel but offering the precision of a spade. It easily cut through the thick main root coming off a parent oakleaf hydrangea yet allowed us to keep the root ball intact for easy relocation to a new site. This model’s compact, efficiently designed head and comfortable grips also make this a good choice for those with impaired strength and mobility, but the high price could be a barrier.

Get the Spear Head Spade shovel at Amazon or Spear Head Spade.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 3.5/5; Comfort 3/5; Performance 4/5; Value 4/5

Short-handled shovels are useful when working in tight spots, and with this mini shovel, gardeners can easily dig holes, move dirt, apply compost, or remove stubborn weeds. This flat-head shovel has a strong metal shaft, a rust-resistant steel head with a sharpened edge, and a D-shaped nonslip grip to keep your hands from cramping during work. The entire tool measures just shy of 30 inches and weighs less than 2 pounds.

When this small shovel arrived, we first thought it was a toy. It’s shorter than our main tester’s shirt sleeves, and when the blade is buried in the soil, the top of the handle is only knee-high. But as we used it in our garden, we were surprised by how sturdily built it is. It’s lightweight enough to use one-handed and feels almost like an oversized trowel (or undersized spade). For most adults, it will be best for tasks like preparing soil in large containers or doing up-close work (on hands and knees) in raised beds. The Z&G mini spade would make an outstanding first garden spade for a child.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Comfort 5/5; Performance 4.6/5; Value 4/5

Whether the goal is to slice through thick roots, neaten up the edges of the lawn, or move a pile of compost or soil, this Fiskars flat-top garden spade is up to the task. This extremely sturdy spade weighs under 5 pounds yet has a steel shaft, a hardened steel blade, and an extra-large D-shaped handle that’s big enough for both hands. It also features a nonslip grip that increases comfort when cutting through compacted soil and clay or slicing through dense sod.

The shaft on this spade is a bit longer than average, which is great for taller gardeners. However, since the shaft and the rest of this shovel are steel, it would be nice if it also had a built-in steel handle instead of an attached one made of polyresin that could fail over time. Also, while the tool is welded, the metal around strong welds can break if stressed excessively. Still, so long as it’s only needed for moderate-duty tasks, this will be an excellent and likely long-lasting choice.

What our tester says: “We really like this spade’s oversized D-handle, longer shaft length, and reinforced blade. It’s more comfortable and less fatiguing than our old garden spade for tasks like digging in soil or moving dirt. “—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Fiskars spade shovel at Ace Hardware or Walmart.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Comfort 4/5; Performance 4/5; Value 4.6/5

If you need to scoop and move garden fertilizer, mulch, soil amendments, lightweight gravel, or even a bit of snow, this Ames garden scoop is an excellent choice. It weighs under 5 pounds and features a rustproof aluminum alloy blade that curves up at the sides and back, helping it handle large loads without difficulty. It also has a 26-inch hardwood shaft that’s topped with a soft, comfortable D-shaped handle with a nonslip grip.

In some ways, the Ames scoop shovel was difficult to test. Unlike the other shovels in our lineup, it’s not really the type of shovel you’d generally reach for when working with soil. However, we ended up using it to load compost and mulch onto a wheelbarrow from our driveway, and we were incredibly happy with how quickly we were able to complete the task. It worked like a giant transfer shovel, with the oversized scoop head and flat edge making it extremely easy to collect the relatively lightweight particles. Farmers, homesteaders, and serious gardeners will appreciate this tool for working with soil amendments, fertilizers, and animal feed by the cubic yard.

Get the Ames D-handle shovel at The Home Depot or Acme Tools.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Comfort 5/5; Performance 4/5; Value 5/5

Gardeners who work in raised beds or plant lots of seedlings know the value of a good garden trowel. The Fiskars Ergo Trowel is a lightweight, inexpensive tool made of rust- and corrosion-resistant cast aluminum. Its ergonomic cushioned hand grip has a textured nonslip coating for sure-handed gardening.

Despite the fact that our testers have vastly different hand sizes, this trowel felt comfortable in hand for us both. We found it useful for planting 4-inch seedlings in garden soil and repotting a range of houseplants, but the trowel’s edge wasn’t sharp enough for us to create clear divisions in clumps of oregano and thyme. Also, although cast aluminum resists rust and corrosion really well, it is a brittle material that breaks easily. To avoid damage, we didn’t test this trowel for tasks like prying up established perennials or turning previously untilled soil. However, this is an excellent choice if you need a medium-duty trowel for working in established garden beds or with potted plants.

Get the Fiskars trowel shovel at Amazon, Target, or Blain’s Farm & Fleet.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Comfort 5/5; Performance 4/5; Value 4.3/5

This True Temper post hole digger is designed to penetrate and loosen compacted soil and clay before removing it in preparation for fence posts, deck footers, and more. Its durable steel blades open when the handles are together and form a closed scoop when pulled apart, allowing you to create perfectly round vertical holes without leaving loose dirt behind. Thanks to its lightweight steel-reinforced fiberglass handles, this post hole digger only weighs about 9 pounds. One handle has a built-in ruler for accurate depth measurement, and both are topped with high-visibility yellow cushion grips that increase control and comfort.

We tested this tool while installing a row of twenty 4×4 fence posts 30 inches deep. We appreciated the smooth functioning of the pivot hinge and the fact that this model weighed less than the wood-handled model we’d used before testing. While the fiberglass handles transmitted slightly more vibration and shock than the wood-handled version, we did find them more comfortable to grip.

What our tester says: “Having used a few post hole diggers in our time, we were incredibly happy this model’s handles didn’t pinch our hands like others we’ve used. It also comes at a great price, which is nice since it’s a single-task tool.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the True Temper post-hole shovel at Acme Tools.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Comfort 5/5; Performance 4/5; Value 4.3/5

A flat shovel is the best tool for moving piles of bulky material or cleaning up ice or mud from pavement—and we wanted to test the True Temper square-point shovel for these tasks because of its light weight and durable construction. The steel head on the True Temper features a wide step and open back secured to a hardwood handle with a steel ferrule for added strength. The hardwood handle not only reduces weight but also absorbs shock and vibration, making scraping and cleanup tasks more comfortable.

In our tests, the hardwood handle stood out for its general comfort. It’s light, slightly flexible, and naturally easy to grip, especially with bare hands. The shovel performed well when moving soil, mulch, and gravel on both paved and unpaved surfaces.

True Temper also offers this shovel with a fiberglass handle or a shorter D-handle, which may be preferable for stabilizing heavier loads like gravel. However, we found this long-handled version to be an excellent all-purpose tool. A flat shovel is one of those tools you may not realize you need until you have one, and this model proves that point.

Get the True Temper square-point shovel at Amazon.

The collection of shovels we tested was diverse, and some models are designed for highly specific tasks. To give each model a fair shake, we planned different tests for each shovel type and sometimes used more than one shovel to complete a certain project.

To test the digging shovels, trench shovel, and garden spade, we removed sod and turned soil for a new garden bed. Since we were in the middle of a fence post installation project, we swapped out our old post hole digger for the one in this guide. That same project left us with mounds of soil to remove from the ground adjacent to the installed posts—a perfect job to test the flat shovel. We also transplanted a tree with the tree-planting shovel, planted seedlings with the trowel, and worked up a raised bed with the mini spade.

Once our tests were complete, we rated each tool’s abilities. The shovels that made our list will meet the demands most homeowners would expect, including periodic heavy-duty use.

Before choosing one of the best gardening shovels for your maintenance tasks, consider which shovel type, material construction, length, weight, and grip will work best. With a bit of advanced planning, you can select the best gardening tool for your needs.

While most people have experience with a round-point or flat-head shovel for all-purpose digging, there are actually many more types of shovels to consider. Shovel type is based on blade shapes, handle design, and purpose and includes digging shovels, trenching shovels, tree-planting shovels, edging shovels, mini shovels, trowels, spades, scoops, and post hole diggers.

Almost all digging shovels and garden spades have steel blades. Steel is heavier and more durable than aluminum. While aluminum is prone to denting and bending, it is less expensive and better at resisting rust. If you are considering a shovel with steel blades, look for models with a rust-resistant coating.

Low-end shovels generally have stamped steel blades, meaning the blade and attachment to the shaft were machine-stamped from a sheet of steel. High-quality shovels have forged blades, meaning the blade started as a single piece of heated steel that was then hammered into shape. Forged steel blade tools are more expensive, but they also last longer.

Also, take note of the socket where the handle is inserted into the blade (head). Forged shovel heads have a solid socket with no seam, which makes for an extremely strong attachment. Stamped shovel heads have a narrow opening or seam at the back. If there is a seam, it may be reinforced either by welding or with a steel ring at the top called a collet. The seams on some shovels are not reinforced.

Garden shovels, spades, and scoops usually have a shaft between 44 and 48 inches long, which is a comfortable length for most people. There are also shorter shovels and spades, with shafts measuring between 18 and 24 inches in length. Longer shafts generally provide better leverage and are easier on the user’s back. When working in a confined area, a short shovel is usually the better choice.

The most common shaft materials for shovels are wood, fiberglass, and steel.

Well-designed shovels have a handle and grip that provide good traction, protect against blisters, and limit hand fatigue. On longer tools, the grip is most often made of heavy plastic or rubber. Ergonomic tools have a textured grip, providing a more secure hold on the shovel.

Some shovels simply have a grip built into the shaft, others have a D-shaped or round handle, and a few have textured grips on both the shaft and the handle. D-shaped and round handles allow you to grasp the top of the shovel with one hand and the shaft with another for more leverage.

Most full-length garden shovels and spades weigh between 4 and 6 pounds, while some handheld tools weigh 2 pounds or less. Shovels containing fiberglass and aluminum fall on the lower end, while wood and steel shovels have more weight.

Consider a shovel’s weight carefully. A shovel may be heavier due to the materials that make it more durable in tough applications. While the extra weight might be worth it in some situations, a few extra pounds can make a noticeable difference after several hours of yard work. Ultimately, the ideal weight depends on the user’s strength and endurance.

Shovels are simple tools, but they come in a wide range of types and sizes that make them appropriate for a variety of tasks, including gardening, planting bushes or shrubs, and digging fence postholes. For more information about these common gardening tools, review the following commonly asked questions and their answers.

Designed with a fiberglass handle and a forged steel blade to penetrate and break through thick roots, the Bully Tools 12-Gauge Round Point Shovel is one of the best options for digging up roots buried deep in the lawn or garden.

To get tips on how to store shovels, we reached out to Michael Clarke, landscape architect, horticulturalist, and founder of Yardwork. According to Michael, “Shovels are best stored by hanging on a wall. This allows them to be up and out of the way so there is less chance for them to slip and fall onto something nearby. Additionally, they are more protected from water that can cause rust and damage if allowed to pool around the head of a shovel.”

The best material for a shovel will depend on the project it’s needed for. Many shovels and professional gardening tools are made with steel since steel is strong and durable. However, steel tools can be heavy. Aluminum shovels are lighter, less expensive, and better at resisting rust, but they are prone to denting and bending.

Michael Clarke, founder of the online nursery Yardwork, recommends sharpening a shovel for a garden two or more times per year, depending on use. “Sharp shovels are able to break through the ground better, divide perennials and shrubs easier by slicing through roots quickly, and move through thick materials like mulch and debris,” he says.

Yes, cleaning a shovel after use can prevent it from rusting or accidentally spreading disease. In our guide on how to care for garden tools, we detail the ideal process, which includes removing dirt with a wire brush, disinfecting with diluted bleach, removing rust with vinegar, and oiling wooden handles.

Mark Wolfe is a writer and product tester with a background in the nursery and landscaping industry. For more than 20 years he mowed, edged, planted, pruned, cultivated, irrigated, and renovated beautiful landscapes. #7681. This Christmas Chimney Decor Is Cute—But Is It Dangerous? Experts Weigh In

A homemade Santa chimney display uses cardboard and pool noodles, but a roofing expert warns that this holiday craft could put a home at risk.

The holidays are a great time to put up decorations around the home, either purchased decor or DIY options. Social feeds are full of ideas, but are all of them good or safe?

A recent viral video on a homeowner’s roof made it look like Santa is climbing into the chimney. It’s a creative chimney hack that might appeal to homeowners decorating for Christmas. But placing cardboard and other craft materials on a roof raises some safety concerns, especially during winter.

Learn what a roofing expert says about the potential fire hazards, moisture problems, and safer alternatives.

Not according to Andre Kazimierski, co-owner and president of HomeHero Roofing, a residential roofing company in Illinois.

“That decoration is definitely not wise to be putting up on your roof,” Kazimierski says. “Not only is it a fire hazard, but it’s likely going to create issues with moisture.”

The cardboard and foam used in the decoration can catch fire, especially if they’re close to a working chimney. “Cardboard is flammable, so if it manages to catch on fire, it can then easily spread that fire to your roof,” Kazimierski warns.

Chimneys release heat and sometimes sparks, which could ignite nearby decorations. There’s also a risk of cardboard or other materials blocking the chimney opening, allowing smoke or dangerous gases to enter the home. Even if the fireplace isn’t in use, the chimney could still vent another heating appliance.

Rain and snow present another problem. “Cardboard can absorb a lot of water and get really soggy,” Kazimierski says.

Wet cardboard can collapse against the roof, while the paper covering and other decorations may start falling apart. Kazimierski warns that trapped moisture could also lead to mold, damaged roofing materials, or unwanted pests.

Moisture is already a concern for brick chimneys. “Common brick is like a sponge, absorbing water and wicking moisture to the chimney interior,” according to the Chimney Safety Institute of America. “Defective mortar joints or the use of improper mortar or brick can greatly increase the tendency to absorb and convey water to the interior of the masonry chimney structure.”

A wet cardboard display resting against the chimney could keep the surrounding area damp, adding to existing moisture concerns.

Homeowners who want to decorate their roofs for Christmas should be careful about how they attach decorations. Nails and screws can puncture shingles, allowing water to seep underneath and potentially cause leaks.

Roofing manufacturer GAF recommends avoiding nails or staples when installing holiday decorations. Large displays can also damage shingles or come loose in strong winds.

Climbing onto the roof to install or remove decorations carries its own risks, particularly when the shingles are wet or covered in snow or ice.

For homeowners who want to recreate the Santa chimney decoration, a safer option is to build a freestanding display on the porch or in the yard, away from the home’s actual chimney. Weather-resistant materials will hold up better than cardboard, and a sturdy base can help keep everything in place during windy weather.

If the display includes lights, the National Fire Protection Association recommends using decorations rated for outdoor use and checking electrical cords for damage.

Keeping the decoration at ground level also makes it easier to inspect, maintain, and remove without climbing onto the roof.

#7678. Waymo Is Banned From California Freeways, For Now — Here’s Why

California ordered Waymo off freeways after troubling encounters with road crews and police. Here's what happened and how riders are affected.

Driving through a construction zone can be confusing, especially when lanes are closed or police are directing traffic. Waymo’s self-driving cars have run into problems in these situations, too.

On Nov. 11, California banned Waymo from operating driverless vehicles on freeways following several incidents involving road crews and police. The company has since stopped freeway rides in other states as well.

Here’s why California stepped in and what the ban means for Waymo passengers.

The California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) said the incidents put construction workers and other drivers at risk.

On Nov. 5, three Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on Highway 101 near Burlingame, where crews were working. Waymo said no one was injured, and no collisions occurred.

The next day, another Waymo attempted to pass California Highway Patrol vehicles during a traffic break on Interstate 280. Officers use traffic breaks to slow or stop vehicles, often because of roadwork or a hazard ahead. Drivers must stay behind the patrol cars until officers allow traffic to resume.

Waymo had similar problems in May, which led to a temporary suspension and software changes. But new incidents occurred in November.

In April, California approved stricter rules for self-driving cars. DMV Director Steve Gordon said the changes would bring “additional accountability for AV manufacturers.”

The freeway ban doesn’t affect Waymo’s regular street service, although some trips may take longer. Waymo has also voluntarily stopped commercial freeway rides in other states while it looks into what went wrong.

Waymo’s cars use cameras and sensors to monitor traffic, but construction zones don’t always follow normal traffic patterns. The recent incidents showed problems with how the vehicles responded to road closures and police activity.

There’s no date yet for Waymo to return to California freeways. The DMV wants the company to show that its cars can safely handle road closures and police activity before allowing driverless freeway rides again.

Waymo says it’s working with state officials and will continue testing on freeways with trained specialists behind the wheel. Passengers can still book rides on regular streets in the meantime.

#7675. Has That Final Destination Truck Scene Ever Actually Happened in Real Life?

Here's what real-world crash data actually says about the likelihood of a Final Destination truck scene.

Giving drivers a reason to fear logging trucks since 2003, Final Destination 2 opened with one of the franchise’s most visceral—and memorable—scenes. A logging truck traveling down a busy highway spills its cargo and sets off a chain reaction of intense car crashes. It’s a gruesome, cinematic disaster, but the basic danger is grounded in reality.  Logs can come loose during transport, with serious consequences on a busy road.  Has anything like the Final Destination truck scene actually happened in real life?

Yes, there have been real-life incidents where logging trucks lost their cargo and caused major highway accidents. However, the Final Destination truck scene depicting this realistic road hazard is grossly exaggerated. Logs can fall off of trucks and cause accidents, but they don’t bounce down the highway and become windshield-level projectiles like in the film. So, yes, the danger is real, but the chain-reaction chaos depicted in the film is highly dramatized.

In January 2024, a logging truck on Interstate 95 in Florida overturned while traveling too fast through a curve in the road. Logs spilled onto the highway, rolled over a barrier and into oncoming traffic. A Jacksonville man who was involved in the accident told local reporters, “I just had a real life Final Destination moment…” However, he and all other motorists were unharmed. In June of 2025, another turnover dumped not logs, but large metal pipes across Highway 75 in Tulsa, Oklahoma, closing both lanes of traffic. Again, no injuries were reported. A fatal accident involving a logging truck did occur in Arkansas in 2014. While traveling down Highway 65, the truck blew a rear tire, swerved into a bridge construction site and tipped over. Two construction workers were killed by the discharged logs.

Each year, shifting or unsecured loads carried by commercial vehicles are linked to roughly 4,000 to 7,000 accidents. This may not sound like a lot, but these accidents have severe consequences, often resulting in serious injury or death. “They regularly make news headlines, so the average person may think they’re more common than they are,” personal injury attorney Juan Dominguez says. In fact, the most dangerous vehicles carrying cargo are non-commercial cars and trucks. 73 percent of highway accidents involving road debris are caused by passenger vehicles with unsecured loads. Commercial trucks are closely regulated and inspected for proper load security, contributing to lower accident rates. Despite the attention given to logging truck accidents, they are only involved in 1.5 percent of all fatal commercial truck accidents each year.

Take control of your safety when sharing the road with large cargo trucks. Here’s how:

“My first rule is to never drive directly behind a truck with a [loose] load like logs, pipes or steel beams,” construction safety specialist Steven Menotti says. “If the load shifts or falls off, you’ll be the first vehicle it hits.” If you have to drive behind a cargo truck,  increase your following distance to at least four seconds, which allows for more reaction time if debris falls into the road. “That distance can help if the unexpected happens and something comes loose,” Dominguez says. “You have more time to try and react.” If possible, reduce your speed for a shorter stopping distance.

If you need to pass a truck on the highway, time it so you can quickly complete the pass and return to the lane. Avoid driving directly next to a cargo truck for an extended length of time to avoid being hit by falling debris or cargo.

If you spot a truck without a properly secured load, move away from it on the road. Look for worn or loose straps and chains, unevenly loaded cargo or missing side stakes. “Those all indicate the trucker probably didn’t check the load,” Menotti says. “I won’t follow it. I change lanes, and pull far back.”

Logs can fall from trucks, but they don’t bounce or become projectiles across the highway like the Final Destination truck scene. In the film, this depiction was CGI-generated.

Brake hard and avoid swerving. Swerving causes 37 percent of all road debris accident fatalities, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).

#7673. Not Horsing Around: Carriage owners file lawsuit to challenge new ban in NYC

A recent New York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators. (Photo from Shutterstock)

A recent New York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators.

The city council passed the ban Thursday, putting an end to a 168-year industry that has attracted a healthy tourist business. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani plans to sunset the carriages by June 1, 2028, in all five boroughs in the city. The union representing carriage operators and owners argues that their livelihood has been taken away and seeks to have the ban struck down.

“The city’s approach can be summarized in 12 words: immediately cripple the owners, ignore property interests and contracts, and maybe compensate,” according to the suit.

Additionally, the new law stipulates the “humane disposition” of the horses. Animal rights activists have in the past expressed concern over the welfare of the horses. Earlier this year, an 18-year-old tourist died after jumping from a runaway carriage—the first fatality since the carriages were introduced into Central Park in New York City.

“Our city has changed, and now it is time for our laws to change, too,” Mamdani said.

#7670. This DIY Coffee Station Can Be Built Using Only Scrap Wood

Give your coffee maker a home with this coffee station organizer.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Clear the counter clutter and fuel your mornings with a scrap-wood coffee station that has a spot for everything.

If you know three things about me, it’s that I’m a stickler for organization, I run on coffee, and I can’t throw away wood scraps. This coffee station checks all three boxes.

It’s built almost entirely from maple offcuts, which explains the mix of thicknesses on the Cutting List. To keep it approachable, every joint is a simple butt joint with glue and brad nails. Biscuits are used only for the glued-up panels. If you can make square cuts and run a nailer, you can build this in a weekend.

[Please insert TA “Coffee_org_case.pdf” here with callouts.]

[Please insert TA “Coffee_org_drawer.pdf” here with callouts.]

Boards wide enough for the top (A) and base (B) are almost impossible to find, so I made the panels by joining several boards with biscuits.

Cut the boards at least 1/2-in. longer and wider than needed. The extra material lets you trim the panels square and to size after the glue dries.

Mark across each joint where you want a biscuit, spacing them 6- to 8-in. apart and about 3-in. from each end. Cut the slots with a biscuit joiner. Be generous with the glue in the slots and along the edges. You want an even bead of squeeze-out so you know you have good coverage. Clamp the panels and keep them flat as they dry.

Once the glue dries, scrape off the squeeze-out and cut the top (A) and base (B) to the final size. Then cut the rest of the parts following the cutting list.

Connect the two sides (C) and the back (E) to the base (B) of the coffee organizer using 18-gauge brad nails and wood glue. Secure the sides so they’re flush with the bottom of the base. Set the back on the base between the sides, flush with the back edges of the base (B) and sides (C).

Cut the pieces for the butcher block (L) and biscuit-join them the same way you did the panels. Again, cut them at least 1/2-in. oversize. That allows for the wood shifting during clamping and leaves enough on each end to make clean, square cuts once the glue has dried.

Once the glue is dry, cut the butcher block to final size on the table saw. Scrape and sand off the dried glue, then round over the sharp edges with a router and a bearing-guided 1/4-in. round-over bit.

When you size the butcher block, leave room for the drawer slides you’ll install later. Most need about 1/2-in. on each side, so a 13-in. opening takes a 12-in.-wide butcher block.

The left-hand compartment houses the butcher block and drawer, so it needs to be 13-in. wide: 12-in. for the butcher block and drawer, plus 1-in. for the drawer slides. Mark the divider location, then test-fit the butcher block and loose drawer slides to confirm the opening. Apply glue and secure the center divider (D) with 18-gauge brad nails driven up through the base (B) and in through the back (E).

Note: Drawer slide clearance varies by style and manufacturer. Check your slides’ specs and adjust the opening as needed.

Build a drawer to store coffee pods and spoons. Glue and nail the drawer box front and back (G) to the ends of the sides (F), then attach the bottom (H) to square it up. The drawer front (K) covers the nails on the front.

Secure the drawer dividers (J) inside the drawer (Fig. B) with wood glue and brad nails, spacing them to fit your coffee pods, spoons, or other items. Feel free to add or take away dividers as needed. I left 1-1/2-in.-wide slots for pods and a 4-in.-wide slot for spoons.

On the left side of the coffee organizer, install the butcher block (L) and drawer using your drawer slides and the included hardware. Both attach to the left side (C) and center divider (D), so install the butcher block first and the drawer above it. Pre-drill and hand-screw for proper alignment and to avoid stripping the screws.

Once the butcher block (L) and drawer are installed, cover the left compartment with the top (A), securing it with glue and 18-gauge brad nails. The right side stays open.

Then attach the drawer front (K) to the drawer box front so it overlaps the left side (C) and center divider (D). Use double-sided tape to position it and 1-in. screws from inside the drawer box to lock it down.

Install and secure dividers on the right side of the unit with 1-1/4-inch 18-gauge brad nails and wood glue. Working from the front to the back of the coffee station:

In the 6-1/4-in. space between the front face (M) and the short divider (N), install the tea separators (R) and spacers (S and T) to make a divided area for sugar, teas, stirrers, etc. Use a 23-gauge nailer and 5/8-in. nails to secure the spacers (S and T) to the front face (M) and short divider (N), then slide the tea separators (R) into the gaps between them. My compartments were 2-1/8-in. and 3-in. wide, but feel free to make them whatever size you’d like.

Sink any protruding nails, fill the nail holes with wood filler, and finish-sand the entire piece. Apply a finish to the whole unit. I used Tried & True Original Wood Finish, which is food-safe, so it works on the butcher block and everything else

Then install the handles on the drawer and butcher block. You can’t reach behind the solid butcher block to drive a screw, so cut the head off the handle screw with a hacksaw, drill a pilot hole, and glue the cut end into it with CA glue or epoxy.

A food-safe wood finish won’t transfer chemicals or toxins to the food when being used. There are two ways a finish is considered food-safe. Either it is completely non-toxic and edible in its liquid state from its origin, or, once fully cured, the VOCs (volatile organic compounds) in the finish disperse, and it becomes a stable, inert, non-toxic solid. Finishes like food-grade mineral oil or fractionated coconut oil are considered food-safe from the time of application and work well as food-safe wood finishes.

A coffee station should include options for coffee or tea, sweeteners, flavoring and stirring. Focus on organization and easy access tiers – no matter what you choose to present in your coffee station.

42-in. works well for a free-standing coffee station cabinet. This is slightly higher than a standard 36-in. countertop height and lower than a 45-in. bar height top. For a coffee station on a countertop beneath upper cabinets, you want enough clearance to open and close your coffee maker’s lid. A 6-in. tall coffee station would give you 12-in. clearance in a standard 18-in. opening between the top of the counter and the bottom of the upper cabinets.

#7667. Second District Court Rules Against Trump's New Birthright Citizenship Executive Order

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Judge Christopher Cooper of the District of DC ruled the order is illegal, and issued a class action injunction blocking it.

Yesterday, in the case of Nathan v. Trump, federal district Judge Christopher Cooper of the District of DC issued a ruling against Trump's new executive order restricting birthright citizenship. The ruling is very similar to an earlier September decision by Judge Boardman of the District of Maryland. The one difference is that the class action injunction in Nathan covers a class that literally consists of all children illegally deprived of birthright citizenship under the new order, whereas the class in the Maryland case is slightly narrower.

I previously  wrote about Trump's new executive order seeking to deny birthright citizenship to various classes of children born on US soil, and noted the first legal challenges to it. As I pointed out then, almost every part of the new order is at odds with the Supreme Court's recent ruling in Trump v. Barbara, which struck down Trump's executive order denying birthright citizenship to children of undocumented immigrants born in the United States, and those born to non-citizen parents here on temporary visas. The Fourteenth Amendment guarantees citizenship to all children "born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof." In Barbara, the Supreme Court majority made clear that "subject to the jurisdiction thereof" includes children of all persons who are subject to and required to obey US law.

Judge Cooper rightly concludes that nearly all the various classes of children barred from birthright citizenship by the new order are in fact protected by the reasoning of Barbara and other Supreme Court precedents, because they and their parents are clearly subject to US law, and required to obey it:

Earlier this year, the Supreme Court struck down President Trump's Executive Order 14160, which purported to deny citizenship to children born to parents temporarily or unlawfully present in the country. Those children, like "nearly all children born in the United States," the Court explained, are "citizens at birth" because they are born "subject to American law." Trump v. Barbara, 609 U.S. 719, 734–37, 740–41 (2026). Barbara reaffirmed that birthright citizenship extends to all but three narrow categories of children, each long understood to be beyond the Nation's governing authority at birth: children of foreign officials enjoying full diplomatic immunity, children of enemy forces in hostile occupation of U.S. territory, and children born aboard foreign public ships.

Yet Barbara's ink had scarcely dried when the President issued a second executive order—Executive Order 14418, at issue here—directing federal agencies to withhold recognition of citizenship from additional categories of U.S.-born children with noncitizen parents. Among those now targeted are children whose parents work for foreign governments or international organizations but lack diplomatic immunity, children born through commercial surrogacy arrangements, and children with a parent suspected of membership in certain gangs or terrorist organizations. As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws. The Court will therefore certify a class consisting of children who are or will be unlawfully denied citizenship under the Order. And it will preliminarily enjoin the Government from enforcing the Order against members of that class.

As explained in my original August post on the new executive order, that order covers four groups almost all of whose members are clearly subject to US law:

Children of "alien enemies," defined as those where at least one of two non-citizen parents is a "designated Foreign Terrorist Organization under 8 U.S.C. 1189 or Specially Designated Global Terrorist, consistent with the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, 50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq., and Executive Order 13224 of September 23, 2001 (Blocking Property and Prohibiting Transactions With Persons Who Commit, Threaten to Commit, or Support Terrorism)."

Children born to at least one non-citizen parent who is a "foreign government employee" or employed by an "international organization that possess[es] international-organization immunity."

Children where "either parent" has engaged in "birth tourist" transactions of various kinds (deliberately seeking to give birth in the US so the child would get birthright citizenship).

Children "born in a territory or territorial waters of the United States where citizenship is not conferred by Federal statute." …[T]his only applies to children born in American Samoa, the one populated overseas US territory to whose residents Congress has not conferred citizenship by statute….

As I explained more fully in my August post, all of the children in these four categories are obviously subject to US law, with the exception of those born to foreign diplomats who have diplomatic immunity. This latter group is already excluded from birthright citizenship. In that post, I also explained why the analogy between "alien enemies" (as defined in the order) and children of members of an invading army occupying US territory fails.

Judge Cooper's opinion analyzes all four categories thoroughly and effectively. He's particularly strong on the case of children of "alien enemies," a category which - he explains - the Trump order defines far more broadly than is justified by legal precedent, and which in any case does not include anyone not "subject to the jurisdiction" of the United States, because all such people are under US control and required to obey US law when on American soil. That differentiates them from the historically recognized exception for children of enemy troops in "hostile occupation" of US territory during a war. The US does not have effective jurisdiction over territory occupied by a hostile enemy army. But the last time any such thing occurred was during World War II, when the Japanese occupied a number of US island possessions in the Pacific.

I noted some additional problems with Trump's "alien enemies" carveout in my August post about the second birthright citizenship order:

Finally, the [order is wrong about] children of "alien enemies," defined…. as members of various designated "terrorist" entities. If they enter the United States, they are subject to US law. That's why they can be prosecuted for any crimes they commit on US soil - including acts of terrorism!

Members of these groups may be bad people. Some have committed horrendous crimes. But that is no reason to visit the sins of the parents upon the children. If a murderer or a rapist has a child born on US soil, the child is entitled to birthright citizenship, notwithstanding the reprehensible behavior of the parents. The same logic applies here.

It is also worth noting that the "foreign terrorist organization" (FTO) designation has been slapped onto various groups that are not actually terrorists in the ordinary meaning of the word, most notably groups engaged in smuggling illegal drugs.

Trump may be trying to use the "alien enemy" designation here to analogize these children to children of members of an invading army, born  at a time and place where the invaders have seized control of US territory, thereby preventing the exercise of US "jurisdiction." Trump v. Barbara reaffirms the longstanding view that such children are excluded from birthright citizenship, because born in an area where US jurisdiction does not (at the time) meaningfully apply.

But FTOs have not, in fact, "invaded" or occupied any part of the United States. Thus, US jurisdiction still applies. Therefore, children of members these organizations are not analogous to children born to members of an occupying foreign army. No part of the United States has actually been invaded and occupied since the Japanese seized various US territories in the Pacific during World War II.

In my article, "Immigration is Not Invasion….," I explain in much more detail why the activities of drug dealers do not qualify as an "invasion," why an FTO designation cannot change that reality, and why courts should not defer to the president's claims that an "invasion" has occurred.

#7666. Sneezing After You Put Up the Tree? You Might Have Christmas Tree Syndrome

A Christmas tree may explain those December sniffles. Learn what Christmas tree syndrome feels like and how to reduce common triggers at home.

Being at home during the holidays can be a magical time of year for many. But for some, it also means dealing with allergies. Christmas tree syndrome could be responsible. Sneezing might start soon after the Christmas decorations go up, sometimes happening around the same time every year.

Dr. Racheal Onah, ND, consulting physician with RealTime Labs, explains what causes it, which symptoms to watch for, and how families can reduce their exposure.

Christmas tree syndrome refers to allergy and asthma symptoms that appear after putting up a Christmas tree or holiday decorations. Onah explains that the term is a nickname, not an official diagnosis, though the reactions are real.

Real Christmas trees can bring mold, pollen, and other allergens into the house. A study published in the Annals of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology identified several types of mold on Christmas trees, including some that can cause allergies.

“Outdoors, molds play a part in nature by breaking down dead organic matter such as fallen leaves and dead trees, but indoors, mold growth should be avoided,” explains the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. “Molds reproduce by means of tiny spores; the spores are invisible to the naked eye and float through outdoor and indoor air.”

Symptoms can include, but are not limited to:

Symptoms that get worse around the tree but improve away from home may point to an allergy. Onah says frequent sneezing and itchy eyes without a fever suggest an allergic reaction rather than a virus. A cold is more likely to bring a fever, sore throat, or body aches.

Onah suggests checking for mold or musty smells before buying a real tree. She recommends having the tree lot shake off loose debris, then rinsing the tree outside and letting it dry before bringing it indoors. Once inside, Onah recommends keeping the tree away from heating vents and running a HEPA air purifier in the same room.

Artificial trees can cause problems, too, depending on where and how they’re stored.

“Artificial trees that sat in a garage or basement for 11 months have had plenty of time to collect dust and moisture,” says Onah. “They are often stored in the original cardboard boxes they came in, which is a material that holds onto humidity and can feed mold on its own.”

Wreaths, garlands, and fabric decorations can collect dust or develop mold in storage as well. Scented candles and artificial snow sprays may also bother people with allergies.

Onah recommends unpacking decorations outside and wiping down artificial branches before setting them up. She says glass, metal, and hard plastic ornaments can be washed with warm water and mild dish soap. Porous decorations with visible mold or a musty smell, such as fabric, paper, or wood pieces, should be thrown away.

“When the season is over, make sure everything is completely dry before you pack it away,” says Onah. “Use sealed plastic bins instead of cardboard, add a few silica gel packets to absorb moisture, and store everything off the floor. If possible, opt to store your bins in a climate-controlled space like an interior closet rather than a garage, attic or basement.”

Anyone dealing with recurring allergy symptoms or worsening asthma should check with a healthcare provider.

“I’d pay extra attention if symptoms linger after the decorations come down,” says Onah. “This could be a sign the decor stirred up a bigger mold problem in the home, like a damp storage area or an HVAC system that’s harboring growth.”

#7665. Blue Wave, Blue Economy—But Not Black and Blue

Wall Street delivered its verdict on the blue-wave midterms 48 hours later in the form of a red wave—red ink, that is.

After a brief relief rally the day after the election, the Dow shed more than 1,800 points, the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell more than 5% and into correction territory, and roughly $2.5 trillion in market value vanished in a single session. Nvidia alone dropped more than 8%.

Market participants watched the collapse of the AI trade in real time—the bet that a massive buildout of data centers, chips, and software would power faster growth, higher productivity and rising wages for years to come. That theory hit the brick wall of an incoming Congress that has AI and data centers on their blacklist.

Democrats, who will comfortably control the Senate and hold their largest House majority in nearly two decades, have been far more hostile to data centers and AI than Republicans have. Several of their biggest wins came in places such as Texas, where local opposition to new data centers had been building.

Investors can read the writing on the wall: more regulation and taxation, slower permitting, and lower profits for AI and AI-adjacent companies. Since equity prices are ultimately justified by future earnings, adjusting those future expectations down also drove down equity prices.

>>> What’s Really Behind the Call to Regulate AI 

The fallout goes well beyond Silicon Valley. AI investment has been a key component of recent growth, and tens of millions of ordinary Americans own these companies through their 401(k)s. A slower buildout means fewer construction jobs, less demand for electricians and engineers, and slower productivity gains that drive real wage growth.

The fiscal picture is dimmer, too. With Democrats running both chambers, there is no chance of further tax reform or meaningful spending cuts for at least two years. If a Republican Congress couldn't bring itself to enshrine the DOGE savings into law, a Democratic one certainly won't.

Instead, Democrat leaders are already promising to restore cost-increasing Obamacare subsidies and unwind recently implemented work-requirement reforms for welfare, all of which will layer new commitments on top of deficits already running at levels once seen only in wartime or recession.

Aside from burdening future generations with debt, these perpetual deficits have consequences for Americans today. The government is crowding out borrowing in the private sector, competing with families and businesses for loanable funds, thereby driving up interest rates on everything from mortgages to student loans to credit cards.

Those higher borrower costs fall especially hard on those Americans that are already in debt and behind financially. The flood of government debt issuance also puts pressure on the Federal Reserve to help finance the debt by creating money to pay for perpetual deficits—a recipe for more inflation.

>>> Slowing Data Center Construction Signals the Need for Pro-Growth Reforms

Unfortunately, a Democratic Congress will also likely offer no help on permitting reform, which is badly needed to build the pipelines, transmission lines and reliable power plants a growing economy requires.

So the outlook is clearly worse, but why isn’t it terrible? Much of the consequential economic public policy changes of the past two years didn't depend on Congress, and it won’t go forward either. And while the tax-reform legislation passed last year obviously did require Congress, most of its provisions are permanent and won’t need reauthorization.

The administration retains broad authority to issue executive orders and roll back burdensome regulations. Cutting that red tape, on everything from energy production to banking, reduces compliance costs for Americans without a single vote on Capitol Hill.

Democrats will certainly try to slow that good work. Their leaders are already planning a wave of made-for-cable show trials that will drain time and attention from officials who should be dismantling the bureaucracy. But investigations can only delay regulatory reform, not stop it.

The president’s veto is another silver lining that will likely prevent the Democratic Congress from enacting sweeping tax hikes or new regulatory regimes. The worst ideas will hopefully die in committee or an Oval Office waste basket.

The economy has weathered worse than a hostile Congress. Ongoing deregulation and existing tax reform are still tailwinds for economic growth while the veto pen is there to stop headwinds as they arise. The outlook might be blue, but it’s not black and blue.

#7664. Plastic surgeon sentenced to death for killing ‘beloved’ lawyer

Lawyer Steven Cozzi, 41, who worked for Blanchard Law, a small law firm in Largo, Florida, went missing in 2023. Dr. Tomasz Kosowski of Florida was convicted of killing Cozzi and sentenced to death Friday. (Photo courtesy of the Largo Police Department)

A Florida judge has sentenced a prominent plastic surgeon to death for the murder of a “beloved” lawyer who went missing in 2023, saying the doctor committed the crime in a “cold, calculated and premeditated manner.”

Pinellas County Circuit Judge Joseph A. Bulone handed down the death sentence Friday to Dr. Tomasz Kosowski of Florida, who was convicted in September of murdering attorney Steven Cozzi, 41, whom he faced in a contentious lawsuit, Law360 reports.

Prosecutors said Cozzi was last seen entering the restroom of his law office in Largo, Florida, in March 2023. Surveillance video allegedly captured Kosowski walking into the law office’s main entrance on the morning that Cozzi went missing, showing the surgeon carrying a backpack and a large box. About two hours later, the video shows him walking out of the building with a different clothes and pulling a large cart covered with a red blanket.

Cozzi, described as a “beloved” person, worked for Blanchard Law, a small law firm specializing in business litigation, bankruptcies and contract disputes. At the time of his disappearance, Cozzi was representing a defendant being sued by Kosowski over medical billing disputes. His body was never found.

#7662. The U.S. Navy Needs a New Battlecruiser. Will It Get One?

Last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding plan called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a new, modern class of battleship. But delivering it faces significant hurdles. The first is realistically addressing the Navy’s shaky shipbuilding track record. The second is surviving the changed political reality in Washington—made more challenging by Trump’s original plan to name the class of warship after himself.

By any name, the battleship addresses critical needs for the U.S. Navy. A modern battleship’s firepower, command and control, and data-fusion capabilities have been proven vital in recent conflicts in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Persian Gulf. Mitigating shipbuilding risks, such as constrained production capacity and the integration of numerous advanced technologies, necessitate a continuous testing regimen that scales up as the ships are built.

The U.S. Navy Could Use a Modern “Battlecruiser” Warship

The unveiling of the battleship comes as the Navy faces the imminent loss of significant at-sea firepower. By 2031, the departures of various submarines, cruisers, and destroyers will see nearly 2,000 missile-launch tubes lost. To blunt this loss, the next iteration of Virginia-class nuclear submarines will carry 28 hypersonic missiles, and the Navy’s unmanned vessels may also begin to carry offensive weapons.

>>> The U.S. Navy Must Build the “Golden Fleet”

The Navy missed an opportunity to address this firepower dilemma with its aborted CG(X) next-generation cruiser program, abandoned in 2011. These forced aging destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers to continue shouldering the air and missile defense responsibilities for carrier strike groups. Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, however, lack the firepower and crew to fully assume the cruiser mission. The Arleigh Burke-class has 96 missile tubes, against 122 on the Ticonderoga-class, and has limited berthing for the needed staff to manage air and missile defenses for the carrier strike group.

In the long term, the Defiant and subsequent battleships are intended to fill this mission and firepower gap. The Defiant, with its added firepower, sensors and crew, will take over the Ticonderoga-class warships’ responsibilities for defending carrier strike groups. The ship will also employ long-range hypersonic missiles in support of carrier air-strike operations to rapidly suppress emerging threats.

The combination of capabilities merged in Defiant with sustained high speeds makes the vessel more closely resemble a battlecruiser—a high-speed battleship able to deliver long-range firepower and defend the carrier strike group from air and missile threats. However, recent battle lessons are creating another critical mission.

The damage inflicted upon U.S. Fifth Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain, and its temporary evacuation due to Iranian missile launches, demonstrates the vulnerability of permanent land-based naval installations to air attack. Moving headquarters to sea is one way to mitigate this danger, and follows a long tradition of numbered fleet command ships. A battlecruiser with robust command and control capabilities can maintain a common operational picture with the warships and unmanned platforms of its numbered fleet, reducing the Navy’s reliance on global communications.

>>> To Build the Golden Fleet

How the Defiant Can Clear the Political Minefield on Capitol Hill

While battlecruisers are needed now, the United States faces numerous constraints that must be navigated before they can join the Golden Fleet. The high build cost of these ships will likely stir substantial resistance from budget-conscious members of Congress; a bill estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be upwards of $23 billion for the first and subsequent ships costing $18 billion each. There are also serious shortages of skilled workers capable of efficiently building such intricate and substantial ships. Moreover, establishing new or expanding existing shipyards to build these battlecruisers requires working through onerous shipbuilding regulations.

Keeping Congress’ support will necessitate reducing the potential for cost overruns and program delays. One way to accomplish this is to use proven technologies and systems in the initial design. Doing this would result in Defiant embracing existing systems to meet its mission requirements the soonest. Integrating systems like the hypersonic missile technologies being developed for the Zumwalt-class destroyers and the new AN/SPY-6 radars being installed in Arleigh Burke-class vessels will further compress production timelines.

In time, the design will need to be improved on through continuous updates—one being the transition to nuclear power to sustain high speeds and pace the aircraft carrier the battlecruiser is intended to protect. One option is using the same A1B nuclear power plant now used in the Ford-class aircraft carriers, given enough time for production to ramp up to support aircraft carrier and battlecruiser production.

Resurrecting the battlecruiser for modern naval missions is a highly ambitious plan, and it may yet fall through. But it is needed to equip the U.S. Navy with the capabilities for fighting a modern naval war across the Pacific.

This piece originally appeared in The National Interest.
